questions.q: What's the core difference between SOC analyst work and security engineering work described in this lesson?
options: There is no real difference — the job titles are interchangeable
SOC analysts design controls while security engineers only respond to alerts
Security engineers work exclusively night shifts while SOC analysts work standard business hours
Security engineers design and build the controls that get monitored, while SOC analysts monitor and respond to alerts from controls that already exist
questions.explain: A security engineer works one layer up from the SOC analyst: deciding what a control should require, instead of reacting to what it produces.

questions.q: How does a security engineer's day-to-day schedule typically differ from a SOC analyst's?
options: SOC analysts only work on long-term projects, never alerts
There is no scheduling difference between the two roles
Less shift-based, interrupt-driven alert response; more sustained, project-based design and implementation work
Security engineers never do any on-call work at all
questions.explain: SOC work is shift-based coverage of an alert queue; security engineering looks more like a build project, with occasional on-call involvement.

questions.q: Why does this course begin with identity specifically, rather than system hardening or network security?
options: Because identity is easier to learn than any other security topic
Because system hardening has nothing to do with identity
Because this course covers topics in alphabetical order
Because identity is the most common foundation underneath enterprise security engineering work — MFA, SSO, Conditional Access, and Zero Trust all depend on it
questions.explain: Nearly every control a security engineer builds in this stage assumes a trustworthy identity layer underneath it.

questions.q: In the "impossible travel" alert example from this lesson, what role does a security engineer play that a SOC analyst does not?
options: Running the exact same shift rotation as the SOC
Designing the detection's risk threshold and deciding whether the policy blocks or just alerts
Never interacting with Conditional Access policies at all
Only ever closing out tickets after an analyst resolves them
questions.explain: The engineer made the upstream decisions — what counts as impossible, what the risk score triggers, block or alert — before the analyst ever saw the alert.

questions.q: What is this course's place in the overall path, according to this lesson?
options: It replaces the need for the Job-Ready Foundation stage
It is the final course in the entire path
It is a standalone course unconnected to any broader path
It opens the Advanced Specialization stage, building on the Job-Ready Foundation stage that came before it
questions.explain: This course opens the path's second stage, Advanced Specialization, right after the Job-Ready Foundation stage closes.
